title: Rav Idi
author: Aharon Hyman

paragraphs: He was the father of the well-known Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi, as explained in Chagigah 5b: Rav Idi, the father (in Ein Yaakov, “the son,” which Hyman calls a scribal error) of Rabbi Yaakov bar Idi, used to travel three months on the road and [spend] one day in the study house, and the Rabbis called him “the one-day student” (Rashi explains: he walked three months from his house to the study house, etc.; Hyman prefers the plain reading that he went trading for three months to seek his livelihood and could come to the study house only one day, as the Maharsha explains). He was distressed … Rabbi Yochanan said to him: “Please, do not punish the Rabbis.” Hyman considers it very likely that what Rabbi Yochanan said to Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Assi in Yevamot 96b — “Why do you not know how to appease, like Ben Idi our colleague?” — refers to Rav Idi, and not to Rabbi Yaakov his son, who was Rabbi Yochanan’s student.

This Rav Idi still merited to receive from Rabbi Chanina, as in Eruvin 57b: “Rabbah said that Rav Idi said that Rabbi Chanina said.” In Eruvin 60b: “Rav Idi said that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said,” and Rav Idi said of it, “These are nothing but words of prophecy.” In Shabbat 49b, “A certain one-day scholar raised an objection to Rava,” and the Arukh explains that it is Rav Idi; Hyman finds it very hard to understand the Arukh’s words, for this Rav Idi lived long before Rava.

notes.text: במטו מינך is a plea, please; Rav Idi is asked not to cause the other Rabbis to be punished. The EinYaakov son versus father correction, BenIdi identification, Maharsha commercial journey reading and chronological objection to the Arukh are Hyman’s positions, not a new identity adjudication.

Chagigah 5b directly names Idi as Yaakov bar Idi’s father, the three-month journey and one day in the academy, followed by Yochanan’s plea not to punish the Rabbis. The passage itself does not establish a commercial purpose. The Rashi/Maharsha readings, Ein Yaakov son/father correction, Ben Idi equation and objection to the Arukh remain attributed.
